fixes.explanation: Nathan, the prophet, tells the king, "Go and do all that is in your heart…" (2 Samuel 7:3). That's a big yes for David's idea. It's the same kind of yes as "Take another cookie, friend, there's plenty."

That's a fair guess, since David was the one who brought up the ark staying in a tent (2 Samuel 7:2). But Nathan doesn't say it. He says, "…for the LORD is with you." (2 Samuel 7:3). The ark's waiting time never comes up in his answer.

The text says the opposite. God asks, "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people Israel, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’" (2 Samuel 7:7). The question points to a no, so True doesn't fit.
That's right. God asks whether He ever said to any of the leaders, "Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?" (2 Samuel 7:7). The question points to a no, so False is the one that fits.

God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." (2 Samuel 7:8). David went from following sheep to ruling a nation. That's a career jump you don't see on a resume every day.

The threshing floor of Nacon is a spot from the ark's journey (2 Samuel 6:6), not the place God says He took David from. In this passage God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock…" (2 Samuel 7:8). The flock is the place He names.

Right. God promises, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning" (2 Samuel 7:10). He says He will provide a place so that they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. That's a big promise for people who've been pushed around.
God says of David's descendant, "He will build a house for My Name…" (2 Samuel 7:13). So God names the builder, and it's David's descendant. That's who gets the job.

A tent is what the ark has now, and David was the one who brought it up (2 Samuel 7:2). But God says David's descendant "…will build a house for My Name…" (2 Samuel 7:13). It's a house, not a tent. I've set up plenty of folding tables in my day, but this is something else.
God says, "I will be his Father, and he will be My son." (2 Samuel 7:14). That's a close family word, right in the middle of a promise about a kingdom. God says it about David's descendant.

God says the opposite. He says, "But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you." (2 Samuel 7:15). Saul was Israel's king before David. David's descendant gets a different promise than Saul did.

Right. God says, "But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you." (2 Samuel 7:15). Saul was the king before David. God sets Saul beside David's descendant, and the descendant gets the promise that stays.

The text doesn't show David arguing about the building. His prayer opens with, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" (2 Samuel 7:18). I think he's looking at the distance he's come, not the project.

It's in his prayer. David says, "…as if this was a small thing in Your eyes, O Lord GOD, You have also spoken about the future of the house of Your servant." (2 Samuel 7:19). In the same prayer he talks about how far God has brought him and what's ahead for his house.

David says, "What more can David say to You? For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD." (2 Samuel 7:20). When God already knows you, you don't have to explain yourself. Me, I'd still try to explain for ten minutes, mustache waving the whole time.

David says God said, "I will build a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:27). Then he adds, "Therefore Your servant has found the courage to offer this prayer to You." When God makes the promise first, praying back gets a lot easier. It's like a friend texting "Door's open, just come in," and suddenly you're not worried about knocking.
